quiz.why: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after day 5 must cover Pseudomonas and MRSA, which cefepime plus vancomycin does. Ceftriaxone with azithromycin is a community regimen covering neither. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and doxycycline are outpatient oral agents.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old woman has 1 day of dysuria and frequency. She is afebrile with no flank tenderness. The resident writes for nitrofurantoin. Two days later she returns with a temperature of 39 C, vomiting, and right flank pain. What is the pharmacologic problem?
choices: Nitrofurantoin is inactivated by an acidic urine
Nitrofurantoin does not reach therapeutic levels in kidney tissue or blood
quiz.why: Nitrofurantoin concentrates in urine but achieves negligible tissue and serum levels, so it cannot treat pyelonephritis. It does cover E. coli well, works within days for cystitis, and is actually more active in acidic urine.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old is found to have fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Blood cultures are drawn. The CT scanner will be free in 45 minutes. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Antibiotics only after the Gram stain result
Lumbar puncture, then antibiotics, then CT
Dexamethasone and antibiotics now, then CT and lumbar puncture
quiz.why: Every hour of antibiotic delay in bacterial meningitis increases mortality, and dexamethasone must go in with or before the first dose to reduce hearing loss and death. Cerebrospinal fluid cell counts, protein, and glucose stay diagnostic for hours, so the tap can follow.

quiz.q: Which addition to ceftriaxone and vancomycin is required for a 74-year-old with suspected meningitis?
quiz.why: Listeria monocytogenes is a real cause of meningitis over age 50, in pregnancy, and in immunosuppression, and cephalosporins do not cover it. Ampicillin does. Azithromycin, metronidazole, and doxycycline do not treat Listeria meningitis.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old man has a temperature of 39.2 C, a heart rate of 128, a blood pressure of 84/50, and a lactate of 5.1 mmol/L with no obvious source. Which bundle element has the strongest time dependence?
choices: Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition
quiz.why: Antibiotics within the first hour after cultures, with 30 mL/kg of crystalloid, are the interventions tied to survival. Imaging helps find the source but does not itself change mortality on the clock, pressors follow fluid unless the patient is periarrest, and procalcitonin does not guide initial therapy.

quiz.q: A 61-year-old with an ejection fraction of 25% is on lisinopril and furosemide. Which addition would be expected to reduce mortality?
quiz.why: Beta blockade with one of the three proven agents and an aldosterone antagonist each independently lower mortality in HFrEF, and an SGLT2 inhibitor would be the next addition. Furosemide relieves congestion without a survival benefit, digoxin reduces only hospitalizations, and amlodipine is neutral.

quiz.q: A patient in acute heart failure has cool extremities, a blood pressure of 86/64, a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L, and diffuse crackles. Which order is most likely to harm?
choices: A doubled dose of IV furosemide with a new metoprolol order
An arterial line and an echocardiogram
quiz.why: Cool skin with a narrow pulse pressure and a rising lactate is cardiogenic shock. More diuresis worsens hypoperfusion and starting a beta blocker removes the remaining inotropy. Dobutamine addresses the pump, ventilation supports oxygenation, and monitoring guides therapy.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old with known pre-excitation presents in atrial fibrillation at 230 beats per minute with wide, irregular QRS complexes and a blood pressure of 96/60. Which order should be refused?
quiz.why: AV nodal blockade in pre-excited atrial fibrillation drives conduction down the accessory pathway and can produce ventricular fibrillation; this applies to diltiazem, verapamil, adenosine, digoxin, and beta blockers. Procainamide slows the accessory pathway, and cardioversion readiness is always appropriate.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic aortic valve and new atrial fibrillation needs anticoagulation. Which is appropriate?
choices: No anticoagulation is needed with a bioprosthetic valve
Apixaban, since the valve is bioprosthetic and not mechanical
Warfarin only, because any valve replacement excludes DOACs
quiz.why: DOACs are contraindicated only with mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis. A bioprosthetic valve with atrial fibrillation is treated like non-valvular atrial fibrillation, where DOACs are preferred. Aspirin does not prevent cardioembolic stroke, and untreated atrial fibrillation at this age carries substantial risk.

quiz.q: Which CHA2DS2-VASc component is worth 2 points?
choices: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
quiz.why: Prior stroke or TIA and age 75 or older are each worth 2 points because they predict recurrence most strongly. Diabetes, hypertension, vascular disease, age 65 to 74, and female sex are worth 1 point each.

quiz.q: A patient takes morphine 15 mg extended release twice daily at home and is admitted needing IV opioids. Which statement guides safe conversion?
choices: Start at the opioid-naive dose regardless of home use
Convert using milligram-for-milligram equivalence between routes
Give the full calculated IV equivalent to avoid undertreating
Calculate the equivalent, then reduce it by 25-50% for incomplete cross-tolerance
quiz.why: 30 mg of oral morphine daily equals about 10 mg IV, but cross-tolerance between opioids is incomplete, so the calculated dose is reduced 25-50% and then titrated. Naive dosing undertreats a tolerant patient badly, and oral and IV morphine are not milligram-equivalent.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old with a hip fracture is repeatedly receiving hydromorphone and is becoming delirious. Which intervention most reduces both pain and delirium?
choices: A fascia iliaca nerve block with scheduled acetaminophen
quiz.why: Regional block plus scheduled acetaminophen reduces opioid requirement, which is the main modifiable driver of delirium in hip fracture. Diphenhydramine and lorazepam both worsen delirium in older adults, and a fentanyl patch is inappropriate for acute pain and takes 12-24 hours to act.

quiz.q: A patient maintained on buprenorphine 16 mg daily presents with an open tibia fracture and severe pain. What is the best approach?
choices: Continue buprenorphine and titrate a full agonist on top, expecting higher doses
Give only non-opioid analgesia because opioids are contraindicated
Give naloxone first to clear the receptors
Stop the buprenorphine so full agonists can work
quiz.why: Buprenorphine does not prevent full-agonist analgesia; it raises the dose required. Stopping it precipitates withdrawal and worsens pain, denying opioids for an open fracture is inhumane, and naloxone would cause severe withdrawal without improving analgesia.

quiz.q: Which analgesic dose of ketamine and route of delivery is correct for severe pain in a normotensive adult?
quiz.why: The subdissociative analgesic dose is 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg infused over 10 to 15 minutes; pushing it quickly causes an unpleasant dissociative reaction. 1-2 mg/kg IV and 4 mg/kg IM are dissociative doses used for induction or extreme agitation.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old with renal colic has a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL and no comorbidities. Which first-line agent is best supported?
quiz.why: NSAIDs reduce ureteral wall inflammation and renal pelvic pressure, and ketorolac outperforms opioids in renal colic with less nausea and sedation. Opioids are second line, and meperidine is avoided because its metabolite normeperidine accumulates and causes seizures.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old with bulimia nervosa and depression asks about an antidepressant that will not cause weight gain or sexual side effects. Which drug is contraindicated in her specifically?
quiz.why: Bupropion fits her stated preferences but is contraindicated in eating disorders because electrolyte disturbance plus a lowered seizure threshold produces seizures. Sertraline and escitalopram are safe and fluoxetine is actually first line in bulimia, and mirtazapine causes the weight gain she wants to avoid.

quiz.q: Three days after starting haloperidol, a 19-year-old develops a forced upward deviation of the eyes and a painfully twisted neck. Which treatment and timeline are correct?
choices: Propranolol `20 mg` orally over the next week
Valbenazine, because this is likely permanent
Benztropine `1-2 mg` IV, with relief expected in minutes
Dantrolene `2.5 mg/kg` IV for the rigidity
quiz.why: Acute dystonia appears within hours to days and reverses within minutes of an anticholinergic such as benztropine or diphenhydramine. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, propranolol treats akathisia, and valbenazine treats tardive dyskinesia which develops over months to years.

quiz.q: A patient on clozapine calls with a fever and sore throat. What is the priority?
choices: Reassure and advise fluids and rest
Obtain an absolute neutrophil count urgently
Increase the clozapine dose to cover stress
Prescribe penicillin for presumed streptococcal pharyngitis
quiz.why: Fever and sore throat in a clozapine patient means agranulocytosis until proven otherwise, and the neutrophil count decides whether the drug stops immediately. Treating it as pharyngitis or reassuring the patient misses a fatal complication, and raising the dose worsens the risk.

quiz.q: Which mood stabilizer requires screening for the HLA-B*1502 allele in patients of Asian ancestry, and why?
choices: Lithium, because of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Carbamazepine, because of Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk
quiz.why: The HLA-B*1502 allele, more common in some Asian populations, markedly raises the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis with carbamazepine. Lithium causes renal and thyroid effects, valproate causes hyperammonemia and teratogenicity, and lamotrigine rash is managed by slow titration rather than genotyping.

quiz.q: A severely agitated patient has already received olanzapine 10 mg IM. The physician now considers lorazepam 2 mg IM. What is the concern?
choices: The pair causes excessive respiratory depression and hypotension
Lorazepam blocks olanzapine at the D2 receptor
quiz.why: Intramuscular olanzapine combined with a parenteral benzodiazepine has caused serious respiratory depression, hypotension, and deaths, so the manufacturer warns against it. The drugs act on different receptors, dystonia is a D2 effect of the antipsychotic alone, and lorazepam is absorbed well intramuscularly.

quiz.q: A 22 kg child needs ibuprofen 10 mg/kg. The bottle is labeled 100 mg per 5 mL. What volume is correct?
quiz.why: 10 mg/kg times 22 kg is 220 mg. The concentration is 20 mg/mL, so 220 divided by 20 is 11 mL. 5.5 mL would deliver half the dose, 22 mL is double, and 2.2 mL is a tenfold underdose.

quiz.q: A 10 kg child in cardiac arrest needs epinephrine. Which order is correct?
choices: `1 mg` IV using the `1 mg/mL` concentration, which is `1 mL`
`0.1 mg` IM using the `1 mg/mL` concentration, which is `0.1 mL`
`0.01 mg` IV using the `0.1 mg/mL` concentration, which is `0.1 mL`
`0.1 mg` IV using the `0.1 mg/mL` concentration, which is `1 mL`
quiz.why: The arrest dose is 0.01 mg/kg IV, which is 0.1 mg for a 10 kg child, drawn from the 0.1 mg/mL concentration as 1 mL. The 1 mg adult dose would be a tenfold overdose, the IM route is for anaphylaxis, and 0.01 mg is a tenfold underdose.

quiz.q: A 15 kg child in shock needs an isotonic fluid bolus. What volume is given?
quiz.why: The pediatric bolus is 20 mL/kg, so 20 times 15 equals 300 mL, repeated as needed while reassessing. 150 mL is 10 mL/kg, 600 mL is 40 mL/kg given at once, and 75 mL is 5 mL/kg, closer to a dextrose dose than a resuscitation bolus.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with croup weighing 16 kg is ordered dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg. What dose is correct?
quiz.why: 0.6 mg/kg times 16 kg is 9.6 mg, below the usual 16 mg ceiling. 16 mg would be the maximum rather than this child's dose, 4.8 mg is half the calculated dose, and 0.6 mg ignores the weight entirely.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has a heart rate of 185, mottled skin, a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and a blood pressure of 88/56. How should the blood pressure be interpreted?
choices: It means vasopressors should precede fluid
It rules out shock and supports observation
It is expected in compensated shock, which still needs immediate fluid
It indicates the cuff is too large
quiz.why: Children maintain blood pressure by raising heart rate and clamping the periphery, so hypotension is a late and ominous sign. Tachycardia with delayed capillary refill is compensated shock and is treated with 20 mL/kg immediately; pressors follow fluid rather than preceding it.

quiz.q: A patient on methadone 80 mg daily is admitted with nausea and pneumonia. Orders include ondansetron 4 mg IV and levofloxacin 750 mg IV. The potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. What is the greatest risk?
quiz.why: Methadone, ondansetron, and levofloxacin all prolong the QT interval, and hypokalemia amplifies it, creating a stack that produces polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. None of these is a strong serotonergic or dopamine-blocking combination, and nothing here raises potassium.

quiz.q: A patient with recurrent torsades de pointes has a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L and a magnesium of 1.4 mg/dL. What is the immediate treatment?
choices: Magnesium sulfate `2 g` IV with potassium repletion
quiz.why: Magnesium terminates torsades even when the level is normal, and potassium is repleted to about 4.0 mEq/L to shorten repolarization. Amiodarone prolongs the QT further and would worsen it, metoprolol does not address the mechanism, and adenosine treats narrow-complex SVT.

quiz.q: A patient on sertraline is given tramadol for back pain. Twelve hours later he is agitated, sweating, and has sustained ankle clonus with a temperature of 38.9 C. Which is the best initial management?
choices: Haloperidol for agitation and cooling measures
Benzodiazepines, active cooling, stopping both drugs, and cyproheptadine if severe
quiz.why: This is serotonin syndrome from an SSRI plus tramadol; benzodiazepines, cooling, and removal of serotonergic agents are first line, with cyproheptadine for severe cases. Haloperidol adds a dopamine blocker and worsens hyperthermia, dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia, and physostigmine is for anticholinergic toxicity.

quiz.q: A patient on warfarin with a stable INR of 2.4 is treated for a skin infection and returns 6 days later with an INR of 7.8 and gum bleeding. Which antibiotic is the likely culprit?
quiz.why: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, the enzyme clearing the active warfarin isomer, and also displaces it from albumin, producing large INR rises. Cephalexin and nitrofurantoin have minimal interaction, and azithromycin is the macrolide chosen precisely because it avoids this problem.

quiz.q: Which combination is the classic outpatient recipe for severe hyperkalemia?
quiz.why: An ACE inhibitor, an aldosterone antagonist, and trimethoprim, which blocks the distal tubule sodium channel much as amiloride does, all retain potassium and stack. Loop and thiazide diuretics with albuterol lower potassium, and the warfarin combination is a bleeding stack rather than a potassium one.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old on lisinopril for 3 years wakes with tongue and lip swelling, no rash, and no itching. Which statement is correct?
choices: Duration of prior use excludes the ACE inhibitor as the cause
This is bradykinin-mediated; antihistamines and steroids are unreliable and the airway is the priority
Epinephrine will reliably reverse the swelling within minutes
An ARB is absolutely contraindicated for life
quiz.why: ACE-inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, which explains the absence of hives and itch and the poor response to histamine-directed therapy. It can begin after years of use, so duration excludes nothing. ARBs are usually tolerated afterward, though they are introduced cautiously.

quiz.q: Two weeks after starting lamotrigine, a patient has fever, a painful spreading rash, and erosions of the mouth and conjunctivae. What is the correct action?
choices: Stop the drug immediately and arrange burn-center level care
Reduce the dose by half and monitor
Treat as a viral exanthem with supportive care only
Continue the drug and add prednisone
quiz.why: Painful rash with erosion of two or more mucous membranes 1 to 3 weeks after a new drug is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and lamotrigine is a classic cause. The drug is stopped permanently and the patient needs burn-center wound and fluid management. Continuing or reducing the dose allows progression to toxic epidermal necrolysis.

quiz.q: A patient on haloperidol for 10 days develops a temperature of 40.1 C, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, labile blood pressure, and a creatine kinase of 8,400 units/L. Reflexes are diminished and there is no clonus. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: Lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, high creatine kinase, and a subacute onset over days on a dopamine blocker is neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Serotonin syndrome comes on in hours with clonus and hyperreflexia, malignant hyperthermia follows an anesthetic within minutes, and anticholinergic toxicity gives dry skin with normal muscle tone.

quiz.q: During induction with succinylcholine and sevoflurane the end-tidal carbon dioxide rises from 36 to 78 mmHg despite doubled minute ventilation, and the jaw is rigid. What is the first drug to give?
quiz.why: Unrelenting hypercarbia with masseter rigidity after succinylcholine and a volatile agent is malignant hyperthermia, and dantrolene blocks pathologic calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Bicarbonate treats the acidosis but not the cause, cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, and another paralytic does not stop the muscle metabolism.

quiz.q: A confused, tachycardic patient has dilated pupils, a temperature of 38.7 C, flushed dry skin, absent bowel sounds, and urinary retention. Which finding most specifically identifies the syndrome?
choices: Dry skin with absent bowel sounds
quiz.why: Dilated pupils, tachycardia, and fever occur in serotonin syndrome, sympathomimetic toxicity, and anticholinergic toxicity alike. Blocked sweating and blocked gut motility, producing dry skin and a silent abdomen, are specific to anticholinergic poisoning; sympathomimetics and serotonin syndrome both cause sweating.

quiz.q: A patient with a bradycardia of 34, a blood pressure of 68/38, and a normal glucose has taken a large quantity of atenolol. Atropine and fluids have failed. Which is the next specific therapy?
choices: Glucagon `3-5 mg` IV followed by an infusion
quiz.why: Glucagon raises intracellular cyclic AMP through its own receptor, bypassing the blocked beta receptor and restoring rate and contractility. Naloxone reverses opioids, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and risks seizures, and fomepizole treats toxic alcohols.

quiz.q: A farmworker arrives with pinpoint pupils, drenching secretions, wheezing, vomiting, and muscle fasciculations. He has received atropine 2 mg twice without effect. What is correct?
choices: Double the atropine every 5 minutes until secretions dry, and give pralidoxime
Give naloxone for the pinpoint pupils
Give physostigmine to reverse the toxidrome
Atropine has a maximum of 3 mg and should be stopped
quiz.why: Organophosphate poisoning often requires tens of milligrams of atropine; the endpoint is dry secretions and clear lungs, not a fixed dose. Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase before it ages. Naloxone does nothing here, and physostigmine would add to the cholinergic excess and worsen the poisoning.

quiz.q: A patient pulled from a structure fire is comatose with a blood pressure of 72/40 and a lactate of 14 mmol/L despite 100% oxygen. Which antidote should be given?
quiz.why: Burning synthetic materials release cyanide, which poisons cytochrome oxidase and produces profound lactic acidosis with hypotension. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide safely and is given empirically. Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, deferoxamine treats iron, and N-acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen.

quiz.q: A patient who took an unknown overdose is seizing, hypotensive, and has a QRS of 152 ms. Which is the correct treatment?
quiz.why: A wide QRS in overdose means sodium channel blockade, classically from a tricyclic, and bicarbonate provides a sodium load with alkalinization to unblock the channel. Flumazenil and physostigmine can both cause seizures or asystole in this setting, and procainamide is itself a sodium channel blocker and would worsen the toxicity.

quiz.q: A patient on glipizide keeps dropping her glucose to 40 mg/dL despite repeated dextrose ampules. Which addition is indicated?
choices: Insulin with dextrose to stabilize the level
quiz.why: Each dextrose bolus stimulates the sulfonylurea-primed beta cell to release more insulin, creating a cycle. Octreotide suppresses that insulin release. Glucagon depends on liver glycogen that is already depleted, hydrocortisone treats adrenal crisis, and insulin would deepen the hypoglycemia.

quiz.q: Which statement about resuscitation fluid choice is best supported?
choices: D5W is an acceptable resuscitation fluid when saline is unavailable
Albumin improves survival in traumatic brain injury
Balanced crystalloid is preferred; large-volume normal saline causes hyperchloremic acidosis
Normal saline is preferred because Lactated Ringer's contains potassium
quiz.why: Balanced fluids cause less hyperchloremic acidosis and kidney injury. The 4 mEq/L of potassium in Lactated Ringer's is below a hyperkalemic patient's own level, so it remains safer. D5W provides free water and no volume expansion, and albumin was harmful in traumatic brain injury.

quiz.q: A patient's potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and magnesium is 1.3 mg/dL. Forty mEq of potassium has already been given with no change. What explains the failure?
choices: Potassium was given too slowly to register
Hypomagnesemia causes continued renal potassium wasting until magnesium is replaced
Serum potassium cannot be corrected without insulin
The laboratory value is falsely low from hemolysis
quiz.why: Magnesium deficiency opens renal potassium channels, so the kidney dumps potassium as fast as it is given. Replacing 2 g of magnesium allows the potassium to correct. Rate does not prevent a level from rising, insulin would lower potassium, and hemolysis falsely raises rather than lowers it.

quiz.q: A patient with a sodium of 110 mEq/L is actively seizing. What is the correct treatment and target?
choices: Rapid correction to `130 mEq/L` within 4 hours
Normal saline at `250 mL/h` until sodium is `135 mEq/L`
`3%` saline `100-150 mL` bolus aiming for a `4-6 mEq/L` rise, staying under `8 mEq/L` in 24 hours
quiz.why: Seizures from hyponatremia are treated with small hypertonic saline boluses that raise sodium 4 to 6 mEq/L, which stops seizures without exceeding the 8 mEq/L daily ceiling that prevents osmotic demyelination. Isotonic saline is too slow for a seizing patient, restriction is far too slow, and rapid full correction causes permanent injury.

quiz.q: Norepinephrine has been titrated to a high rate in a septic patient whose mean arterial pressure remains 52 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Give 4 L of normal saline rapidly
Increase norepinephrine indefinitely and take no other action
Add vasopressin `0.03 units/min` and search for source control, low ionized calcium, acidosis, or an obstructive cause
quiz.why: Vasopressin adds a non-adrenergic mechanism and is catecholamine sparing, while a rising requirement should trigger a search for an undrained source, hypocalcemia, severe acidosis, tamponade, or adrenal insufficiency. Phenylephrine alone is weaker in distributive shock, and unguided large-volume saline worsens acidosis and edema.

scenarios.title: The first hour of septic shock
scenarios.intro: A `78`-year-old woman is brought in from home by her daughter for two days of confusion and shaking chills. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of `1.6 mg/dL`. Her home medications include lisinopril, spironolactone, metformin, and atorvastatin. She is warm, flushed, and mumbling. You are helping the resuscitation team.

steps.prompt: She is placed on the monitor. She answers her name but not the year. Her skin is hot, and there is left flank tenderness. The team is deciding what happens in the next five minutes.

choices.text: Draw two sets of blood cultures and a lactate, then give broad antibiotics and start `30 mL/kg` of balanced crystalloid
choices.feedback: Correct. Cultures first because they take seconds, then antibiotics within the hour, then volume. That order preserves the diagnosis without delaying treatment.

choices.text: Hold antibiotics until the urine culture and CT result return so the drug can be chosen precisely
choices.feedback: Harmful. Every hour of delay in septic shock raises mortality measurably. Empiric therapy is started now and narrowed later when the culture names the organism.

choices.text: Start norepinephrine immediately before any fluid
choices.feedback: Acceptable only if she were peri-arrest. In a patient who has had no fluid yet, volume comes first, with pressors started if she stays hypotensive during or after the bolus.

choices.text: Give a `500 mL` bolus and reassess in an hour before committing to more
choices.feedback: Too slow. The initial target is `30 mL/kg`, roughly `2 L` for this patient, given quickly, with reassessment during rather than an hour later.

steps.prompt: The team wants antibiotics now. The likely source is the urinary tract but she was hospitalized six weeks ago for a foot ulcer. Her chart lists a penicillin allergy recorded as `rash as a child`.

choices.text: Vancomycin plus cefepime, after clarifying that the childhood rash was not hives, swelling, or wheeze
choices.feedback: Correct. Recent hospitalization raises the risk of resistant gram-negatives and MRSA. A remote childhood rash is not an IgE allergy, and cephalosporin cross-reactivity with a true penicillin allergy is only about `1%` to `2%`.

choices.text: Nitrofurantoin `100 mg` orally, since the source is urinary
choices.feedback: Harmful. Nitrofurantoin reaches no meaningful tissue or blood level, so it cannot treat pyelonephritis or bacteremia. It also cannot be given to a confused, hypotensive patient by mouth.

choices.text: Ceftriaxone `1 g` alone
choices.feedback: Reasonable for community pyelonephritis in a well patient, but it misses Pseudomonas and MRSA in someone recently hospitalized and now in shock. Broader coverage is chosen first, then narrowed.

choices.text: Avoid all beta-lactams entirely and use aztreonam plus vancomycin
choices.feedback: Defensible if she had documented anaphylaxis, but a childhood rash does not justify abandoning the better drug. Ask what actually happened and how quickly before narrowing your own options.

steps.prompt: Two litres are in. Her pressure has come up briefly and fallen again. The lactate came back at `4.8 mmol/L` and the potassium at `6.1 mEq/L`. The ECG shows peaked T waves.

choices.text: Calcium gluconate `1 g` IV now, then insulin with dextrose, and start norepinephrine
choices.feedback: Correct. Calcium stabilizes the myocardium within minutes without lowering potassium at all; insulin with dextrose shifts it over `15-30` minutes. Meanwhile the persistent hypotension after adequate volume is an indication for norepinephrine.

choices.text: Give sodium polystyrene sulfonate and recheck the potassium in four hours
choices.feedback: Far too slow for ECG changes. Binders remove potassium over hours; a widening QRS can become a cardiac arrest in minutes.

choices.text: Give insulin and dextrose alone and hold calcium since the QRS is still narrow
choices.feedback: Peaked T waves are already an ECG change. Waiting for a wide QRS before giving calcium removes the margin you are trying to preserve.

choices.text: Continue fluid boluses only, assuming the pressure will follow
choices.feedback: She has had `30 mL/kg`. Further fluid without a dynamic assessment mostly produces edema; this is the point where a vasopressor is started.

steps.prompt: Norepinephrine is running through a good antecubital IV while central access is prepared. The rate keeps climbing and the mean arterial pressure sits at `58 mmHg`. Her ionized calcium is low and her pH is `7.18`.

choices.text: Add vasopressin `0.03 units/min` at a fixed rate, replace calcium, and look for an undrained source with a CT of the abdomen and pelvis
choices.feedback: Correct. Vasopressin works through a non-adrenergic receptor and is catecholamine sparing. A climbing requirement is a prompt to look for a cause: low ionized calcium, acidosis, and above all an obstructed, infected kidney that needs drainage.

choices.text: Keep increasing norepinephrine and change nothing else
choices.feedback: Escalating a single catecholamine while ignoring hypocalcemia, acidosis, and a possible undrained source is how a shock patient is lost slowly.

choices.text: Switch from norepinephrine to phenylephrine to reduce the heart rate
choices.feedback: Phenylephrine is pure alpha with no inotropy and is a weaker choice in distributive shock. It is used when tachyarrhythmia is the limiting problem, not as a routine substitution.

choices.text: Add hydrocortisone `200 mg` per day and continue norepinephrine
choices.feedback: Reasonable and often done in vasopressor-dependent septic shock, but it is an adjunct. It does not replace searching for the source or correcting calcium and acidosis.

steps.prompt: CT shows an obstructing `8 mm` stone with a dilated, infected left kidney. Urology is called for emergent stent placement. As the team hands off, the daughter asks whether her mother's home medications should be restarted.

choices.text: Hold lisinopril, spironolactone, and metformin, and explain that they contributed to the potassium and the acidosis
choices.feedback: Correct. Lisinopril and spironolactone stack on potassium, and metformin accumulates in kidney injury and worsens lactic acidosis. All three are held until perfusion and renal function recover.

choices.text: Restart everything tonight so her chronic conditions stay controlled
choices.feedback: Harmful. Restarting two potassium retainers and metformin in acute kidney injury is how the same emergency returns.

choices.text: Hold only the metformin and continue the rest
choices.feedback: Half right. Metformin must be held, but leaving lisinopril and spironolactone running keeps the potassium problem alive in a patient with acute kidney injury.

choices.text: Tell the daughter medication decisions are not something you can discuss
choices.feedback: A missed opportunity. You can explain what is being held and why in plain language and direct specific questions to the physician; families understand the plan better when someone says it clearly.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: in the first hour of septic shock the order is cultures, antibiotics, and `30 mL/kg` of balanced fluid, with the antibiotic chosen from where the patient has been, not just where the infection is. Hyperkalemia with ECG changes gets calcium first, then insulin with dextrose. When a pressor requirement climbs, stop turning the dial and go looking: ionized calcium, acidosis, adrenal insufficiency, and above all an undrained source. No antibiotic cures an obstructed, infected kidney; the stent does. Finally, the home medication list that helped cause the crisis (an ACE inhibitor, an aldosterone blocker, and metformin) is part of the treatment plan, not background noise.

scenarios.title: Converting the opioid dose without hurting anyone
scenarios.intro: Work through a conversion the way it happens on a real shift. A `54`-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is admitted with a pathologic femur fracture. At home he takes `morphine sulfate extended release 30 mg by mouth twice daily`, plus `oxycodone 5 mg` up to four times daily for breakthrough, which he has been using every dose for a week. He can no longer swallow reliably and needs intravenous analgesia. Anchor everything to oral morphine milligram equivalents, where `30 mg` oral morphine is the reference unit.

steps.prompt: First, total his daily oral morphine equivalents. Extended-release morphine `30 mg` twice daily is `60 mg`. Oxycodone `5 mg` four times daily is `20 mg` of oxycodone. What is his total?

choices.text: `60` plus `30` equals `90` oral morphine equivalents, because `20 mg` oxycodone equals `30 mg` oral morphine
choices.feedback: Correct. Oxycodone is roughly `1.5` times as potent as oral morphine, so `20 mg` of oxycodone is `30 mg` of oral morphine. His total is `90` oral morphine equivalents per day.

choices.text: `60` plus `20` equals `80`, treating oxycodone as equal to morphine
choices.feedback: This undercounts. Oxycodone is more potent per milligram than oral morphine, and treating them as equal will leave him underdosed on the new regimen.

choices.text: `60` only, because breakthrough doses are not counted
choices.feedback: Incorrect and a common error. He is taking every breakthrough dose, so it is part of his daily requirement and must be counted.

choices.text: `60` plus `60` equals `120`, treating oxycodone as twice morphine
choices.feedback: Overcounts. The conversion is `20 mg` oxycodone to `30 mg` oral morphine, a factor of `1.5`, not `2`.

steps.prompt: Now convert `90` oral morphine equivalents per day to intravenous morphine. Recall that `30 mg` of oral morphine equals `10 mg` of IV morphine.

choices.text: `30 mg` of IV morphine per day
choices.feedback: Correct. Dividing by three gives `30 mg` IV morphine per `24` hours, which is the raw calculated equivalent before any safety adjustment.

choices.text: `90 mg` of IV morphine per day, since the routes are equivalent
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Oral morphine has only `25%` to `30%` bioavailability, so the IV dose is about one third of the oral dose. This error is a threefold overdose.

choices.text: `10 mg` of IV morphine per day
choices.feedback: Too low. That is the equivalent of `30 mg` of oral morphine, which is one third of what he is actually taking.

choices.text: `45 mg` of IV morphine per day
choices.feedback: This uses a 2:1 oral to IV ratio. The accepted ratio is 3:1, so the correct figure is `30 mg`.

steps.prompt: The team wants hydromorphone instead, because morphine metabolites accumulate and his creatinine is `2.1 mg/dL`. Recall that `1.5 mg` of IV hydromorphone equals `10 mg` of IV morphine. What is the next step after calculating?

choices.text: Calculate `4.5 mg` of IV hydromorphone per day, then reduce it by `25%` to `50%` for incomplete cross-tolerance
choices.feedback: Correct. `30 mg` IV morphine divided by the 10:1.5 ratio is `4.5 mg` of IV hydromorphone. Tolerance does not transfer completely between mu agonists, so the starting dose becomes roughly `2.5` to `3.5 mg` per day, divided and titrated.

choices.text: Give the full calculated `4.5 mg` per day without reduction
choices.feedback: Risky. The full calculated dose of a new opioid in a tolerant patient is a recognized cause of oversedation, because cross-tolerance is incomplete.

choices.text: Start the standard opioid-naive dose of `0.2 mg` as needed
choices.feedback: Harmful in a different direction. He has been taking `90` oral morphine equivalents daily. A naive dose leaves a man with a pathologic fracture in agony and is not safer.

choices.text: Keep morphine rather than converting, since the math is simpler
choices.feedback: Understandable, but morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates in kidney failure and causes delayed sedation. Hydromorphone or fentanyl is the better choice at this creatinine.

steps.prompt: The plan is hydromorphone `0.5 mg` IV every `4` hours scheduled, with `0.5 mg` as needed for breakthrough. The attending asks what else should be on the order set to reduce the opioid requirement.

choices.text: Scheduled acetaminophen `1000 mg` every `6` hours, a bowel regimen, and consideration of a nerve block
choices.feedback: Correct multimodal thinking. Acetaminophen lowers the opioid requirement, a block can substantially reduce it, and constipation is the one opioid effect that never develops tolerance, so the bowel regimen starts with the opioid, not after the problem.

choices.text: Add ketorolac `30 mg` IV every `6` hours
choices.feedback: Tempting, and NSAIDs are excellent in bone pain, but his creatinine is `2.1 mg/dL`. If an NSAID were used at all it would be `15 mg` and briefly; here the kidney argues against it.

choices.text: Add diphenhydramine `25 mg` every `6` hours for itching
choices.feedback: Scheduled antihistamines add sedation and delirium risk without treating pain. Treat itching if it appears, and remember hydromorphone releases less histamine than morphine.

choices.text: Nothing else; a single opioid keeps the regimen clean
choices.feedback: Single-agent opioid therapy needs higher doses for the same relief and produces more sedation, nausea, and constipation than a multimodal plan.

steps.prompt: Six hours later he is comfortable but sleepy, with a respiratory rate of `8` and a pulse oximetry of `91%` on room air. He rouses to voice.

choices.text: Hold the next dose, apply oxygen and stimulate him, and prepare diluted naloxone in `0.04 mg` increments if he deteriorates
choices.feedback: Correct. He is rousable, so the first moves are holding the dose, oxygen, and stimulation. If naloxone becomes necessary, small increments titrated to a respiratory rate of `10` avoid dumping a tolerant cancer patient into withdrawal and severe pain.

choices.text: Give naloxone `2 mg` IV push immediately
choices.feedback: Harmful here. A full dose in a tolerant patient causes violent withdrawal, uncontrolled pain, vomiting, and occasionally pulmonary edema, in a patient who is still rousable and protecting his airway.

choices.text: Continue the schedule unchanged because the pain is finally controlled
choices.feedback: A respiratory rate of `8` with falling saturation is the warning that precedes apnea. Comfort does not justify ignoring it.

choices.text: Hold the dose and simply recheck in an hour without oxygen or stimulation
choices.feedback: Holding is right, but passive observation wastes the interval. Oxygen, stimulation, and continuous monitoring are what make the hold safe.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry: every opioid conversion is three steps. Total the daily oral morphine equivalents including breakthrough doses actually taken, convert to the new drug and route using the table anchored at `30 mg` oral morphine, then cut the result by `25%` to `50%` because cross-tolerance between mu agonists is incomplete. Route matters as much as drug — oral morphine is only about one third as available as IV. Kidney function picks the agent: morphine metabolites accumulate, so hydromorphone or fentanyl is safer. Multimodal therapy lowers the opioid dose needed, and a bowel regimen starts on day one. When sedation appears, the response is graded: hold, oxygen, stimulate, and only then dilute naloxone into `0.04 mg` steps titrated to breathing rather than to wakefulness.

scenarios.title: The slow heart with no story
scenarios.intro: Rescue brings in a `63`-year-old man found unresponsive at home by his son. No witnesses, no note, no empty bottles found. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation. His son says he has been depressed since his wife died and lists his medications from memory: `metoprolol`, `amlodipine`, `apixaban`, and `amitriptyline` for sleep. Blood glucose on arrival is `88 mg/dL`.

steps.prompt: He is unresponsive to voice, breathing shallowly at `8` per minute. Pupils are mid-sized. The monitor shows a wide-complex bradycardia. What happens first?

choices.text: Open the airway, assist ventilation with a bag-valve-mask, get a `12`-lead ECG, and establish two large IVs
choices.feedback: Correct. Airway, breathing, and circulation come before any antidote, and the `12`-lead ECG is the single most informative test in an undifferentiated overdose because QRS width decides the next drug.

choices.text: Give naloxone `2 mg` IV immediately for the low respiratory rate
choices.feedback: Reasonable reflex and unlikely to hurt, but his pupils are mid-sized and no opioid is on the list. Naloxone is worth trying, yet it cannot come before airway support and the ECG.

choices.text: Give flumazenil `0.5 mg` IV to reverse presumed sedative overdose
choices.feedback: Harmful. With a tricyclic on the medication list, flumazenil can strip GABA inhibition and precipitate seizures that benzodiazepines can no longer treat.

choices.text: Start transcutaneous pacing before anything else
choices.feedback: Premature. Pacing may be needed, but ventilation and an ECG come first, and pacing frequently fails to capture in drug-induced bradycardia until the toxin is addressed.

steps.prompt: The `12`-lead shows a rate of `36`, a QRS of `148 ms`, and a tall terminal R wave in lead aVR. He then has a `45`-second generalized seizure.

choices.text: Sodium bicarbonate `1-2 mEq/kg` IV push, repeated until the QRS narrows, plus a benzodiazepine for the seizure
choices.feedback: Correct. A wide QRS with a terminal R in aVR is the signature of sodium channel blockade from the amitriptyline. Bicarbonate provides a sodium load and alkalinization that unblocks the channel; benzodiazepines are the correct anticonvulsant here.

choices.text: Phenytoin `20 mg/kg` for the seizure
choices.feedback: Harmful. Phenytoin is itself a sodium channel blocker and worsens tricyclic cardiotoxicity. Benzodiazepines are first line for toxin-induced seizures.

choices.text: Physostigmine `2 mg` IV for the anticholinergic features
choices.feedback: Dangerous with a QRS of `148 ms`. Physostigmine given in tricyclic overdose has caused asystole. The wide QRS is the contraindication.

choices.text: Amiodarone `150 mg` for the wide-complex rhythm
choices.feedback: Wrong mechanism. This is not a primary ventricular arrhythmia, and amiodarone blocks sodium and potassium channels, which worsens the conduction delay.

steps.prompt: After `150 mEq` of bicarbonate the QRS narrows to `112 ms` and the seizure has stopped. The heart rate is still `40` and the blood pressure `74/42` despite `2 L` of crystalloid. Atropine `1 mg` produced no change.

choices.text: Give glucagon `5 mg` IV followed by an infusion, and start high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy
choices.feedback: Correct. With metoprolol and amlodipine both on the list and atropine failing, glucagon bypasses the blocked beta receptor and high-dose insulin acts as an inotrope in beta blocker and calcium channel blocker poisoning.

choices.text: Give calcium chloride `1 g` through a central line and continue insulin therapy
choices.feedback: Also reasonable, and calcium is specifically useful for the amlodipine component. Glucagon and high-dose insulin remain the broader answer when both drug classes are possible.

choices.text: Repeat atropine every `3` minutes up to `3 mg` and wait
choices.feedback: Atropine rarely works in drug-induced bradycardia because the block is at the receptor, not in vagal tone. Repeating it wastes minutes.

choices.text: Give more bicarbonate until the pH exceeds `7.6`
choices.feedback: Harmful. Bicarbonate is titrated to QRS narrowing with a pH goal of about `7.45` to `7.55`. Pushing beyond that causes hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and arrhythmia without further benefit.

steps.prompt: Glucagon and a high-dose insulin infusion are running with dextrose. The rate is `62` and the pressure `96/58`. The pharmacist asks what monitoring the insulin therapy requires and what other antidote should be available.

choices.text: Hourly glucose and frequent potassium, with lipid emulsion available if the circulation collapses
choices.feedback: Correct. High-dose insulin drives both glucose and potassium into cells, so both are followed closely, and dextrose is infused continuously. Lipid emulsion is the rescue for lipophilic drug cardiotoxicity that does not respond to everything else.

choices.text: No specific monitoring is needed once the pressure improves
choices.feedback: Unsafe. High-dose insulin therapy causes profound hypoglycemia and hypokalemia; these are the complications that harm patients during an otherwise successful rescue.

choices.text: Check glucose once at the end of the infusion
choices.feedback: Far too infrequent. Glucose is checked at least hourly, and often every `30` minutes early in the infusion.

choices.text: Monitor glucose closely but stop replacing potassium, since insulin lowers it safely
choices.feedback: Half right. Glucose monitoring is essential, but insulin-driven hypokalemia still needs cautious replacement; the intracellular shift does not mean the level can be ignored.

steps.prompt: He stabilizes and is admitted to the intensive care unit. The son asks whether the apixaban matters and whether his father can simply be woken up with a reversal drug.

choices.text: Explain that apixaban matters if he bled or fell, that andexanet alfa exists for serious bleeding, and that there is no drug that reverses this overdose as a whole
choices.feedback: Correct and honest. Anticoagulation changes the threshold for head imaging in an unwitnessed collapse, its specific reversal agent is used only for serious bleeding, and most poisonings are treated with supportive care plus targeted antidotes rather than a single reversal.

choices.text: Tell him flumazenil will wake his father shortly
choices.feedback: Wrong and dangerous. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines only, and in the presence of a tricyclic it can cause seizures that are then untreatable with benzodiazepines.

choices.text: Say the anticoagulant is irrelevant because there is no visible bleeding
choices.feedback: Incomplete. An unwitnessed collapse in an anticoagulated patient raises the threshold for head imaging precisely because intracranial bleeding can be occult.

choices.text: Defer entirely and say only that the physician will speak with him
choices.feedback: Acceptable for prognosis, but a plain explanation of which drugs have antidotes and which do not is within scope and helps a frightened family understand what is happening.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: in an undifferentiated overdose the `12`-lead ECG does more diagnostic work than any laboratory test, because QRS width sorts the sodium channel blockers out of everything else. A QRS over `100 ms` with a terminal R wave in aVR means bicarbonate, titrated to a narrowing QRS rather than to a target pH, and benzodiazepines rather than phenytoin for the seizures. Bradycardia that ignores atropine and fluid points to receptor blockade: glucagon for beta blockers, calcium and high-dose insulin for calcium channel blockers, and both when the bottle is unknown. High-dose insulin therapy is effective and demanding, requiring hourly glucose and close potassium monitoring. And two antidotes stay in the drawer: flumazenil and physostigmine, both of which can kill the patient in front of you when a tricyclic is on board.
